units.t: The Human Body. Episode one.
In this episode: The cell: life's building block, Your heart and blood, How breathing works and How digestion works.
Part one. The cell: life's building block.
You are a walking city of tens of trillions of cells, each one a busy factory with its own power stations, post office and instruction library.
Seeing the first cells.
In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through his microscope and saw rows of tiny empty boxes.
They reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in, so he called them cells.
He was seeing the walls of dead plant cells.

Soon after, the Dutch draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who ground his own lenses, found pond water and tooth scrapings swarming with tiny living creatures: bacteria and other single-celled organisms nobody had seen before.
In the late 1830s Schleiden and Schwann argued that plants and animals are built from cells.
In the 1850s Rudolf Virchow popularised the key addition: every cell comes from another cell.
This overturned the belief that life springs from mud or rotting meat, and it let medicine understand disease as something going wrong in cells.
Trillions and a smart border.
Recent estimates put an adult human at around 30 trillion cells, thousands of times more than the number of people on Earth.
Most, by count, are red blood cells: tiny discs with no nucleus, built to carry oxygen.
Some nerve fibres run a metre from spine to foot.
You also carry a similar number of bacteria, mostly in your gut.
Every cell is wrapped in a membrane only a few billionths of a metre thick.
It is a double layer of fatty molecules called phospholipids, with water-loving heads outside and water-avoiding tails inside.
But a cell needs food in and waste out, so the membrane is studded with proteins that act as gates, pumps and messengers.
Some let only certain substances through.
Others receive signals from hormones or other cells.
Inside the factory.
A typical animal or plant cell is crowded with specialised parts called organelles.
The nucleus is the control centre, holding the DNA with instructions for building proteins.
Those instructions are copied and sent out, where ribosomes, tiny molecular machines, read them and assemble proteins one building block at a time.
A folded network called the endoplasmic reticulum helps make and transport many proteins, and the Golgi apparatus packages and labels them for delivery, a bit like a post office.
Mitochondria release energy from food, producing ATP, a molecule that powers almost everything the cell does.
Plant cells also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a stiff wall for support.
Bacteria are simpler cells with no nucleus; their DNA simply floats inside.
Bacteria within us.
One of biology's most surprising ideas is that parts of your cells were once separate living things.
The theory, championed by Lynn Margulis from the late 1960s, says mitochondria began as free-living bacteria.
More than a billion years ago, one cell engulfed another but did not digest it.
The two formed a partnership: the guest supplied energy and the host supplied shelter and food.
Over time the guest became a permanent part of the cell.
The evidence is strong.
Mitochondria have their own small loop of DNA, similar to bacterial DNA, and they divide on their own, much as bacteria do.
Chloroplasts in plants appear to have the same kind of origin, from captured cyanobacteria.
You inherit your mitochondria from your mother.
Dividing, renewing, going wrong.
You began as a single fertilised egg, and every one of your trillions of cells came from that cell dividing again and again.
Before dividing, a cell copies its DNA, then splits so each new cell gets a full set.
This continues throughout life.
The lining of your gut is renewed every few days, and red blood cells last about four months.
Most nerve cells in your brain, however, are thought to last most of your life.
Division is tightly controlled by signals telling a cell when to grow, stop or die.
Cancer is what happens when mutations break those controls, so cells keep dividing when they should not.
Understanding the cell is why modern cancer treatments can target specific faults.
The key idea: Cells were first seen in the 1600s, and cell theory says all living things are made of cells and every cell comes from an existing cell.
Part two. Your heart and blood.
Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, pushing blood through tens of thousands of kilometres of vessels.
A tireless pump.
Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, tilted slightly left, and is about the size of your fist.
Its cardiac muscle resists fatigue.
At rest it beats 60 to 100 times a minute, around 100,000 times a day.
A natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, triggers each beat.
The heart has two upper atria that receive blood and two lower ventricles that pump it out.
The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
The left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body, so its ventricle has the thickest wall.
Four one-way valves keep blood moving the right way, and their closing makes the 'lub-dub' a doctor hears.
Vessels and pressure.
Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle the pressure of each beat; the pulse in your wrist is an artery stretching.
They branch into capillaries, so narrow that red blood cells pass in single file, where oxygen and nutrients move into tissues and waste moves out.
Veins return blood at lower pressure, using one-way valves and squeezing leg muscles.
Laid end to end, an adult's vessels would stretch tens of thousands of kilometres.
Blood pressure, like 120/80, is the force on artery walls: the top number as the heart beats, the bottom between beats.
Persistently high pressure often has no symptoms but damages arteries, so regular checks from a GP or pharmacy matter.
What blood is made of.
An adult has about five litres of blood.
Just over half is plasma, a yellowish liquid carrying nutrients, hormones, salts and proteins.
Red blood cells, made in bone marrow, carry oxygen using haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that makes blood red.
Their flattened disc shape gives more surface area and lets them squeeze through tight capillaries.
White blood cells, far fewer in number, fight infection.
Platelets are cell fragments that clump together to plug wounds and start clotting.
Red blood cells live about 120 days, and your body replaces them at roughly two million every second.
Blood types and donation.
Red blood cells carry markers called antigens.
The ABO system sorts blood into groups A, B, AB and O, and the Rh factor adds positive or negative.
Blood with markers your immune system doesn't recognise can trigger a dangerous reaction, so blood is carefully matched.
O negative can be given to almost anyone in an emergency, so it is always in demand.
AB positive people can usually receive red cells from any group.
In Australia, donations are collected by Australian Red Cross Lifeblood.
One donation is split into parts, such as red cells, plasma and platelets, so it can help several patients.
Feeding and protecting it.
The heart can't feed itself from the blood inside its chambers.
Coronary arteries, wrapped around its surface like a crown, supply its muscle.
Over decades, fatty plaque can narrow them.
If a plaque ruptures, a clot can block the artery, starving the muscle beyond it of oxygen.
That is a heart attack, and fast treatment saves muscle.
Heart disease is a leading cause of death in Australia.
Key risks include smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, inactivity and too much alcohol.
Exercise, plenty of plants and less salt help.
Adults 45 and over, 30 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, can ask a GP for a Heart Health Check.
For chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, or breathlessness, call 000.
The key idea: The heart is a fist-sized pump with four chambers, serving two circuits.
Part three. How breathing works.
You will take around 20,000 breaths today without thinking about any of them.
Here is the clever machinery that keeps the air moving.
Autopilot and diaphragm.
You breathe roughly 12 to 20 times a minute, almost none of them by choice.
Breathing runs automatically yet can be taken over by will: you can hold your breath, sing a long note or blow out candles.
When you stop paying attention, the brainstem quietly takes control back.
Every breath delivers oxygen your cells need to release energy from food, and removes the carbon dioxide they produce.
Lungs have no muscles of their own.
The diaphragm, a dome of muscle beneath them, contracts and flattens, while rib muscles lift the ribcage.
The chest enlarges, pressure inside drops below the air outside, and air flows in.
Breathing out at rest is mostly passive: the diaphragm relaxes and elastic lungs spring back.
In hard exercise, neck, chest and belly muscles help.
Hiccups are sudden spasms of the diaphragm.
A tree, then a swap.
Air passes the voice box, travels down the windpipe and splits into two main branches, one per lung, which divide again and again like an upside-down tree.
The smallest twigs end in tiny air sacs called alveoli.
There are hundreds of millions, giving the lungs an enormous surface.
The right lung has three lobes, the left only two, leaving room for the heart.
The nose warms, moistens and filters the air.
Each alveolus is wrapped in hair-thin capillaries.
Oxygen crosses into the blood and latches onto haemoglobin in red blood cells, while carbon dioxide moves out.
Inhaled air is about 21 per cent oxygen, and exhaled air still has roughly 16 per cent.
That leftover oxygen is one reason rescue breaths during CPR can help someone who is not breathing.
The urge to breathe.
Hold your breath and the urge to breathe becomes overwhelming.
Surprisingly, that urge is not mainly caused by running low on oxygen.
Sensors in the brainstem and major arteries track carbon dioxide in the blood, which also changes its acidity.
When carbon dioxide rises, they push you hard to breathe.
This carries a safety lesson.
Some swimmers and divers hyperventilate before going underwater, blowing off carbon dioxide so they can stay down longer.
The urge to breathe is delayed, but oxygen keeps falling, and a person can black out without warning.
This is a known cause of drowning, even among strong swimmers, so hyperventilating before breath-holding in the water is dangerous and should be avoided.
Built-in cleaning crew.
Every day you breathe in dust, pollen, smoke particles and microbes.
Your airways are lined with sticky mucus that traps particles, and with millions of microscopic hair-like structures called cilia.
The cilia beat in coordinated waves, moving mucus up to the throat, where it is usually swallowed without you noticing.
Scientists sometimes call this the mucociliary escalator.
Coughing and sneezing are the emergency backups, blasting out irritants at high speed.
Cigarette smoke damages and slows the cilia, which is one reason people who smoke often develop a persistent cough: the body must cough up what the escalator can no longer clear.
Bushfire smoke is also hard on airways, so on smoky days it makes sense to follow local health advice.
Breathing and how you feel.
Breathing is closely tied to the nervous system.
When you are anxious, breathing tends to become fast and shallow, and when you are relaxed it slows down.
The link works in both directions, so deliberately slowing your breath, especially with a long, unhurried breath out, can help many people feel calmer.
Exercise does not grow new lung tissue, but it trains the breathing muscles, the heart and the muscles that use oxygen, so everyday activity feels easier.
Lung function naturally declines a little with age, and smoking speeds that decline sharply.
Breathlessness that is new, sudden or worsening deserves attention.
This lesson is general information rather than medical advice, so if you are worried about your breathing, talk to a doctor or check healthdirect, and in an emergency call triple zero.
The key idea: Breathing runs on autopilot via the brainstem, and the diaphragm does the work of drawing air in.
Part four. How digestion works.
From first bite to final exit, your food travels through several metres of tubing and takes a day or more.
Here's what happens along the way.
Mouth to stomach.
The digestive tract is a long tube from mouth to anus, often quoted as about nine metres in an adult.
Chewing breaks food up, and saliva, about half a litre to one and a half litres a day, contains amylase, which starts turning starch into sugar.
That's why bread tastes slightly sweet if chewed long enough.
Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push food down the oesophagus, even if you're upside down.
The stomach is a stretchy muscular bag that churns food with hydrochloric acid, which kills many microbes, and pepsin, which starts digesting protein.
Mucus protects its lining, which renews every few days.
After a few hours, the thick liquid called chyme is released gradually into the small intestine.
The small intestine.
Despite its name, the small intestine is the longest part of the tract, several metres long and a few centimetres wide.
Bile from the liver breaks fat into droplets, and pancreatic enzymes break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into sugars, amino acids and fatty acids.
Millions of finger-like villi, covered in even smaller microvilli, give a huge surface area to absorb nutrients into the blood.
Blood from the gut goes first to the liver, which processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen and removes toxins, including alcohol.
The largest internal organ, it can regenerate remarkably.
The pancreas also makes insulin, which helps cells absorb sugar.
The large intestine.
What's left, mostly fibre, water and bacteria, passes into the large intestine, or colon, about 1.
5 metres long.
Here water and salts are absorbed, turning liquid waste into solid stool, which can take a day or more.
The colon is home to trillions of bacteria, the gut microbiome.
They ferment fibre, produce some vitamins such as vitamin K, and help train the immune system.
Fermenting fibre also makes short-chain fatty acids that help nourish the colon lining.
Researchers are actively studying links between the microbiome and health, though many popular claims go beyond current evidence.
Hunger and fullness.
Your gut and brain talk constantly, through hormones and the vagus nerve.
An empty stomach releases ghrelin, which increases hunger.
As you eat, the stomach stretches and the intestine releases hormones that signal fullness.
Fat tissue releases leptin, which helps regulate appetite over the longer term.
These signals take time to register, which is one reason eating quickly makes it easier to overeat.
Short sleep and stress also affect appetite; short sleep, for example, is linked to stronger hunger.
The gut even has its own vast network of nerves, sometimes called the second brain.
When things go wrong.
Reflux, where acid flows back into the oesophagus, causes heartburn; large meals, lying down after eating and alcohol worsen it.
Many adults make less lactase after childhood, so dairy may cause bloating.
Coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten, affects roughly 1 in 70 Australians, and most don't know they have it.
Irritable bowel syndrome causes pain and changed bowel habits without visible damage.
Symptoms overlap, so see a GP rather than cutting out foods on your own.
Most Australians eat less fibre than recommended.
Vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains keep you regular and feed healthy bacteria.
Seek advice about persistent bowel changes, blood in stool or unexplained weight loss.
Free bowel cancer screening kits are available from age 45.
The key idea: Digestion starts with chewing and saliva, then the stomach churns food with acid.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which idea is part of cell theory?
Answer. Every cell comes from another cell.
Question two. Where does the right side of the heart send blood?
Answer. To the lungs.
Question three. What happens when the diaphragm contracts?
Answer. It flattens and enlarges the chest.
Question four. What is peristalsis?
Answer. Muscle waves that push food along.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
